## The big idea

A pump cannot insist on a flow rate, and it cannot insist on a head — it
offers a **pump curve**, the piping demands a **flow curve**, and the
system runs at their intersection. Everything operational follows from
moving that intersection around… including the failure mode that destroys
pumps: cavitation, which is checked in *absolute* head.

::: {.callout-note}
### The number in charge: the NPSH margin
$\mathrm{NPSH_a} - \mathrm{NPSH_r} > 0$, with comfortable room to spare
(0.5–1 m is a common demand). Both are heads; the first is what your
suction line *delivers* in absolute terms, the second is what the pump
*requires*. (Next unit adds a second ruling number, the specific speed
$N_s$, which picks the machine itself.)
:::

## Two curves, one operating point

Write the head equation from reservoir 1 to reservoir 2 and collect what
the piping *demands* from the pump at each flow:

$$H_\text{a}(Q) = \underbrace{\Delta z + \frac{\Delta p}{\rho g}}_{\text{static head}}
\; + \; \underbrace{H_\text{L,maj}(Q) + H_\text{L,min}(Q)}_{\;\propto\, Q^2\ \text{(turbulent)}}$$

That's the **flow curve**:[^syscurve] it starts at the static head (the toll
you pay before anything moves) and climbs like $Q^2$. The pump, meanwhile,
offers its **pump curve** — head falling as flow rises, a fact of
centrifugal life you'll derive in Unit 10. The pump cannot deliver a
$(Q, H)$ pair off its curve, and the system cannot accept one off its own.
The only $(Q, H)$ acceptable to both is the intersection, and that is where
the system runs. Not negotiable; solvable.

[^syscurve]: Pump catalogs call this the *system curve* — same object,
industry name. We'll use both.

So how do you change the flow? You can't order the pump to do it — you must
move a curve. Close a valve: the flow curve steepens (you added $K_L$), the
intersection slides **up and to the left**: less flow, more head, and —
here is the vote-splitter from class — typically *less* power for a radial
machine, since shaft power tracks $\rho g Q H_\text{a} / \eta$ and $Q$ fell
faster than $H$ rose. Throttling is cheap to install and expensive to run:
you're buying less water at a higher price per liter. (The homework makes
you price it against a variable-speed drive. Bring a calculator and mild
outrage.)

## Play with it

A pump ($H = 40 - 9\times10^4 Q^2$, in m and m³/s) fills an elevated tank
through 60 m of 80 mm steel pipe. Move the curves; watch the intersection
obey.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof z2_84 = Inputs.range([0, 35], {value: 12, step: 1, label: "Tank elevation z₂ (m)"})
viewof K_84 = Inputs.range([0, 60], {value: 0, step: 2, label: "Throttle valve K_L"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - z2_84
#|   - K_84
w = water(20)
sys = PipeSystem(fluid=w, z1=0, z2=z2_84)
pipe = Pipe(L=60, D=0.080, roughness='commercial_steel')
if K_84 > 0:
    pipe.add_fitting(K=K_84)
sys.add(pipe)
pump = Pump.from_coeffs(h0=40, a=9e4, efficiency=0.70)
sys.add(pump)

Qs = np.linspace(1e-6, 0.022, 120)
H_pump = [pump.head(q) for q in Qs]
H_flow = [sys.static_head() + sys.head_loss(q) for q in Qs]

try:
    Qop = sys.solve_flow()
    Hop = pump.head(Qop)
    P = w.rho * 9.81 * Qop * Hop / 0.70
    ok = True
except Exception:
    ok = False

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
ax.plot(np.array(Qs)*1000, H_pump, lw=2.5, color='crimson', label='pump curve (offered)')
ax.plot(np.array(Qs)*1000, H_flow, lw=2.5, color='steelblue', label='flow curve (demanded)')
if ok and Qop > 0:
    ax.plot(Qop*1000, Hop, 'o', ms=12, mfc='gold', mec='k', zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(f"  operating point:\n  {Qop*1000:.1f} L/s at {Hop:.1f} m\n  shaft power ≈ {P/1000:.2f} kW",
                (Qop*1000, Hop), fontsize=9)
    ax.set_title("the system runs where the curves cross — nowhere else")
else:
    ax.set_title("no intersection: this pump cannot lift this tank at all")
ax.set_xlabel('Q (L/s)'); ax.set_ylabel('head (m)')
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_ylim(0, 48)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Three experiments. **Throttle** (raise $K_L$) and watch $Q$, $H$, and the
power annotation — squeeze the flow, spend less. **Raise the tank** and
watch the flow curve translate upward until, past ~40 m, the curves stop
crossing: static head has exceeded shutoff head and the pump simply cannot,
at any flow, do the job. **Compare the two moves**: throttling *steepens*
the demand, elevation *lifts* it — different geometry, different remedies.

The steepness distinction settles a real purchasing question. A second
identical pump in **series** stacks the pump curves vertically (heads add);
in **parallel**, horizontally (flows add). Whether either is worth the
money depends entirely on the flow curve it meets: against a steep,
friction-dominated curve, parallel pumping buys almost nothing (the extra
flow drowns in $Q^2$ losses), while series can help; against a flat,
static-dominated curve, the verdict flips. Sketch it before you spend.

## Cavitation: the check that saves the pump

The suction side of a pump is the low-pressure point of the entire system:
the pump has taken its cut of lift and friction *before* adding anything
back. If the absolute pressure there falls to the liquid's vapor pressure,
the liquid boils at pipe temperature — and the bubbles, swept into the
impeller's high-pressure zones, collapse hard enough to hammer metal out of
the blades. The check is done in heads, and in **absolute** terms (vapor
pressure is physics; gauge zero is a bureaucratic convention):

$$\mathrm{NPSH_a} = \frac{p_\text{abs,suction}}{\rho g} + \frac{U^2}{2g} - \frac{p_v}{\rho g}
\;\; \ge \;\; \mathrm{NPSH_r} + \text{margin}.$$

$\mathrm{NPSH_r}$ comes off the manufacturer's chart; $\mathrm{NPSH_a}$ you
compute from the suction line — and the toolbox does it from the components
upstream of the pump (`sys.npsh_available(Q)`, `sys.check_cavitation()`).
The levers, in order of a troubleshooter's checklist: lower the pump / raise
the tank (buy elevation), fatten and shorten the suction line (stop wasting
head before the pump), and *watch the temperature* — between 20 °C and
60 °C, water's vapor pressure grows almost ninefold, quietly eating the
budget. A system that runs cold and fails hot has a classic diagnosis.

::: {.column-margin}
One more practical limit: a pump near shutoff moves almost no fluid, and
the fluid is what carries away the pump's own heat. Manufacturers publish a
minimum continuous flow — respect it, so that the pump is not destroyed.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"A bigger pump means more flow." The system gets a vote. Against a steep
flow curve, a pump twice the size may buy a few percent more flow — and an
oversized pump runs far from its best-efficiency point, wastes power, and
cavitates more readily. The professional question is never "how big a
pump?" but "*where do the curves cross?*"
:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** In the demo, throttle from $K_L = 0$ to 40 and note the power. Explain the direction of the change without equations, in two sentences a plant manager would accept.</summary>
The valve made the pipework a harder customer, so the pump settled at less
flow and slightly more head. Since power is roughly flow × head, and flow
fell by more than head rose, the motor draws less — but every liter now
costs more energy than before.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Why must the cavitation check use absolute pressure when everything else in this course happily uses gauge?</summary>
Boiling happens when absolute pressure meets vapor pressure — a property of
the liquid that doesn't know or care where the local atmosphere set gauge
zero. A gauge reading of −70 kPa means opposite things in Boulder and in
Miami; the liquid responds only to the absolute number.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** A 300 m drip-irrigation run (friction-dominated) needs 40% more flow. Series or parallel second pump — and why?</summary>
Series. The flow curve is steep, so the extra head from stacked pump curves
converts into meaningful flow; a parallel pump's added capacity would be
eaten almost entirely by the $Q^2$ friction wall. (Flat, tank-lifting
systems reach the opposite verdict.)
</details>
